newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya-Ethiopia mourn top cameraman "Mo" Amin.
newsitem.headline: Kenya-Ethiopia mourn top cameraman "Mo" Amin.

text.p: Kenya and Ethiopia on Monday paid tribute to top cameraman Mohamed "Mo" Amin, who died aboard a hijacked plane that crashed in the Indian Ocean.
The Ethiopian government paid glowing tribute to the Kenyan cameraman, saying "Mr Amin will always remain in the hearts and minds of Ethiopians as a true and dedicated friend."
"Ethiopia wishes to express profound sympathy and condolences over the untimely death of Mr Amin in an air crash," the foreign ministry said in a statement in Addis Ababa.

The Ethiopian foreign ministry said it recalled Amin's "unforgettable service to the Ethiopian people when the country was hit by drought and famine in 1984 to 1985 by alerting the international community about the plight of the Ethiopian people, thereby influencing emergency assistance".
The foreign ministry said it was not lost on the Ethiopian people or government that Amin lost part of his left arm covering an explosion in Addis Ababa in 1991.
"Since his love for Ethiopia has always brought him (back) to Addis Ababa on a regular basis, he was returning last Saturday from Ethiopia when he lost his life," it added.

In Nairobi, the Presidential Press Service said: "President Moi noted that although Amin commanded international recognition, he remained humble and pursued his photojournalism profession with single-mindedness."
Moi said he shared the grief of Amin's family "during these trying moments".
In 1994, Moi bestowed on Amin the Order of the Grand Warrior for his professional distinction. It is the highest honour ever given to a journalist in Kenya.
Amin, of Reuters Television, was widely acclaimed for bringing Ethiopia's catastrophic famine in 1984 to world attention.

His first dramatic pictures of the starving and dying jolted the world into a huge relief effort that included a big-name "Live Aid" rock concert beamed around the globe, raising millions of dollars to ease the famine.

Amin, 53, was on an Ethiopian Airlines Boeing 767 seized by three hijackers on a flight from Addis Ababa to Nairobi on Saturday. The airliner ran out of fuel and went down in the sea just off the Comoro Islands.
Only 52 out of the 175 passengers and crew survived.

Amin, who lived in Nairobi, was regarded as one of Africa's top photojournalists. He won numerous awards in a career that spanned four decades after he started out with a camera as a 13-year-old schoolboy covering the East African car rally.
